In our last session ([Lesson 1](lesson1.qmd)), we read in and manipulated our data set, and merged
in NDVI (greenness) data by census tract. This week's module is about **research questions,
conceptual frameworks, and descriptive analysis** — you've already worked through hypothesis
components (exposure, outcome, population, expected relationship) and the mediator-vs-modifier
distinction in this week's "Learn" material. This tutorial is the **Practice** half: hands-on
descriptive statistics, data cleaning, and visualization in R.

That's not busywork. Every study population, exposure, and outcome needs to be *characterized*
before it can be modeled — and this week's skills are exactly what you'll need for **Project
Milestone 1** (research question, hypothesis, and conceptual framework), due this week. Milestone 1
asks you to start characterizing the exposure and outcome you're considering for your own project,
using this same class dataset. Everything below — checking distributions, spotting errors,
visualizing a relationship — is directly reusable for that.

Note that we're reading in **`class_data_processed.csv`**, which already has the NDVI data linked
in from Lesson 1.

In RStudio, that's:

```r
data <- read.csv(file.path("data_processed", "class_data_processed.csv"))
```

In the browser, the chunk below fetches that file for you and puts it in a `data_processed/`

# Why Explore Data Before Analyzing It?

It's tempting to skip straight to the "real" analysis — but exploratory data analysis (EDA) isn't
a formality before the real work starts. **It *is* part of the real work.** Before you can trust
any regression result later in the course, you need to know your data cold: what each variable
looks like, where the errors are, and what a "normal" value even is for each one.

This class dataset is a simulated example of something very real in environmental epidemiology:
data assembled from **multiple sources**, each with its own error patterns. Here, individual-level
answers came from a household survey, and neighborhood-level measures (tree canopy, traffic,
poverty, crime) were **linked in** by census tract — the same kind of linkage you did yourself in
Lesson 1. Every data-collection method has its own way of introducing error:

* **Surveys / interviewer-administered questionnaires** — recall bias, misunderstood questions,
  data entry mistakes.
* **Monitors and administrative/electronic data** — instrument drift, missing readings,
  records that were never meant for research use.
* **Linked data** (like the tract-level variables here) — mismatched geographic identifiers, or a
  value that's technically correct but describes the *neighborhood*, not the *person*.

Broadly, the errors EDA is designed to catch fall into three buckets:

1. **Missing data**
2. **Logical inconsistencies** — combinations of values that can't both be true
3. **Outliers** — values so extreme they're more likely to be errors than reality

We'll work through each of these in turn.

::: {.callout-note}
One more framing note before we start: everything in this lesson is **descriptive**, not
**inferential**. We're not running hypothesis tests or looking at p-values here — we're looking at
distributions to understand the data and catch problems *before* any modeling starts. That
distinction matters enough that it's worth stating explicitly: descriptive analysis characterizes
what's in front of you; inferential analysis (coming later in the course) is what lets you draw
conclusions and test hypotheses from it.
:::

## Checking for Missing Values

Missing values can affect analysis, so it's essential to check for them.

```{webr-r}
# Use the is.na() function with colSums() to count missing values in each column.
missing_values <- colSums(is.na(data))
missing_values
```

**Questions to consider:**

* What variables have missing values?
* How many missing values do you see for each?
* Do you think this is a problem? Why or why not?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Compare against the codebook — click to reveal"}
The [Data Codebook](codebook.qmd#known-missingness-in-this-dataset) lists the missingness that was
deliberately built into this simulated dataset: `mental_health` (42), `current_smoker` (20),
`high_blood_pressure` (12), `stress` (7), `has_park` (5), `age` (3), `gender` (2). If your
`colSums(is.na(data))` output matches that, your merge from Lesson 1 didn't introduce (or lose)
any missingness — which is exactly the kind of check worth doing after any merge.

**A caveat specific to this class exercise:** we can check against the codebook here only because
this is a teaching dataset, built with a known amount of missingness baked in on purpose. With
real-world data, you typically *don't* know in advance how much missingness you have, or where —
you find out by running exactly the code above and looking at the result. A codebook for a real
dataset will usually tell you what a variable means and how it's coded, but not necessarily how
much of it is missing in the specific file you were handed.
:::

For now we will not recode any of our missing variables. In some cases it makes sense to recode
missing variables — particularly if we can infer their values from other variables in the data
frame — but for now we'll proceed without doing that. It's good to be aware of which variables
have missing values, since we'll need to think about this later when conducting analyses.

Since you'll be working with these data in your project analysis, be sure to take note of the
variables that have missing values.

## Checking for Logical Inconsistencies

Missing data is easy to spot — R shows you `NA` directly. **Logical inconsistencies** are sneakier.
When there's a logical inconsistency, every individual value can look perfectly plausible on its
own — it's only when you look at two variables *together* that you find a combination that can't
both be true. A classic example from environmental health survey data: someone recorded as
biological sex "male" who also reports an age at first menstruation. Neither value looks wrong in
isolation — the problem only shows up when you look at both at once.

The tool for catching this is one you already know: `table()`, applied to *two* variables instead
of one, to see every combination that actually occurs in the data.

As a quick illustration of the technique (not a real inconsistency — just showing the mechanics),
let's break age into two rough groups and cross it with gender. We'll use the same approach Lesson
1 used to create `r_age` and `num_education` — `ifelse()`, checking a condition and returning one
value if it's `TRUE`, another if it's `FALSE`:

```{webr-r}
age_group_demo <- ifelse(data$age < 40, "Under 40", "40 or older")
table(age_group_demo, data$gender)
```

**What's happening here:** `ifelse(data$age < 40, "Under 40", "40 or older")` checks every value of
`data$age` — wherever it's less than 40, it returns the text `"Under 40"`; everywhere else, it
returns `"40 or older"`. That gives us a new vector of labels the same length as `data$age`, which
we store as `age_group_demo`. `table()` then cross-tabulates that new label against `gender`, one
count per combination.

Reading a two-way table like this: each cell is a count of people with *that* combination of both
variables. If a cell that should be logically impossible has a nonzero count, that's your signal
to investigate.

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn"}
Let's build a real check, not just an illustration. Think about `education`: is it *possible* for
someone to have a Bachelor's degree at age 20? Sure — early admission, an accelerated program, it
happens, though it's uncommon. What about age 19? Now it's genuinely rare — not a strict logical
impossibility the way "male" + "reports menses" is, but rare enough that finding several such
cases in one dataset should make you suspicious of a coding error, not assume you've found a bunch
of prodigies.

Using the same `ifelse()` pattern as above, build a two-way table crossing an "under 19 / 19 and
older" age split against `education`.
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here — two-way table of an age<19 split against education

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Solution — click to reveal"}
```{webr-r}
age_group <- ifelse(data$age < 19, "Under 19", "19 or older")
table(age_group, data$education)
```

The "Under 19" row should show **0** people with "Bachelor's degree or higher." Unlike the strict
logical-impossibility example earlier (menses age recorded for someone coded male), this isn't a
constraint that's *guaranteed* to hold in every real dataset — it's a "should be at or near zero;
investigate anything that isn't" check. That distinction matters: not every consistency check has a
clean yes/no answer, and part of the skill is judging how surprising a violation would actually be.
:::

## Summary Statistics

The `summary()` function provides a quick look at key statistics (e.g., min, max, median, mean) for
the variables in our data frame.

**This is a quick review from Lesson 1** — you ran `summary(data)` there too, on the raw,
pre-merge data. It's worth doing again here, for two reasons: it's good practice to re-run basic
checks like this after *any* merge (to make sure nothing shifted unexpectedly), and `data` now has
one additional column, `X2015_NDVI`, that you haven't summarized yet.

```{webr-r}
summary(data)
```

**Question to consider:** What descriptive statistics do we see for each of the variables? For
what types of variables does the `summary()` function not provide good information? (If this feels
familiar, it should — see if your answer matches what you found in Lesson 1.)

Now let's redo this, looking only at the numeric variables.

```{webr-r}
# Select only numeric columns in the data
numeric_data <- data %>% select(where(is.double))

# Get summary statistics for only the numeric columns
summary(numeric_data)
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Note:** `is.double()` selects only columns stored as double (continuous numeric variables). This
avoids including integer columns (like `id` and `year`), which are used for identifiers or years
rather than quantities we'd summarize with a mean. Use `is.numeric()` instead if you want to
include both integer and double types — `is.double()` is appropriate here because we want to
calculate means, medians, etc. on genuinely continuous measures. It doesn't make sense to compute
a mean or median for a binary yes/no variable — for those, we need a different tool, which is
exactly what the next section covers.
:::

**Questions to consider:**

* What is the median age in this population? What is the minimum age? What is the maximum age?
* For what variables do we not see much difference in value across the population? Why do you
  think this is?
* What can you tell about percent living in poverty in participants' neighborhoods, based on the
  distribution you see here?

Now let's create some tables to start looking at distributions for the other variables in the
data set.

```{webr-r}
# Identify non-numeric columns (excluding double-precision numeric, id, and year)
non_numeric_data <- data %>% select(-where(is.double), -id, -year)
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Note about the code above:** this selects all columns that are *not* double-precision numeric
(`is.double`), and also removes `id` and `year`. "Double precision" refers to how continuous
numbers are stored in R — they use more memory to allow for decimal values with high precision.
The minus sign (`-`) is used inside `select()` to exclude columns. We're storing the non-numeric
columns in a data frame called `non_numeric_data`.
:::

## Frequency Tables

Now let's create frequency tables to look at other variables:

```{webr-r}
table(non_numeric_data$education)
table(non_numeric_data$stress)
table(non_numeric_data$employment_status)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn"}
Use the same approach (`table()`, and if you like, `prop.table()`) to look at the distribution of
**`race_ethnicity`** in this newly merged dataset. Do the proportions look the same as what you
found for `race_ethnicity` back in Lesson 1? They should — merging in NDVI shouldn't have changed
any of the original columns. If your numbers don't match, that's worth investigating!
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here — distribution of race_ethnicity

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Solution — click to reveal"}
```{webr-r}
table(data$race_ethnicity)
prop.table(table(data$race_ethnicity)) * 100
```
:::

We can also use a function to run this for *all* of the non-numeric variables at once:

```{webr-r}
# Use lapply to create frequency tables for each non-numeric variable
distribution_tables <- lapply(non_numeric_data, function(x) {
  if (is.factor(x) || is.character(x) || is.logical(x) || is.integer(x)) {
    counts <- table(x, useNA = "ifany")             # Frequency counts including NAs
    percentages <- prop.table(counts) * 100         # Calculate percentages
    result <- cbind(Count = counts, Percentage = percentages)  # Combine counts and percentages
    return(result)
  } else {
    return(NULL)
  }
})

# Display the tables for each variable
distribution_tables
```

::: {.callout-note}
You're not expected to write a function like this on your own yet. Save this code (consider
building yourself a small code library of "recipes" like this one) and reuse it whenever you need
frequency tables for every categorical variable in a data set at once.
:::

Take a look at `asthma` in the output above. Its prevalence should look like a plausible
proportion of the population — a small minority, not nearly everyone. That's worth pausing on: a
variable whose distribution looks *implausible* (way too common, way too rare, or suspiciously
uniform) is itself a signal worth chasing down, the same way a missing-value count or a failed
logical-consistency check is.

## Visual Exploration of Data

Tables and summary statistics are useful, but it can also be very helpful to *visually* inspect the
distribution of a variable — some patterns (an outlier, an unexpected cluster, a skew) are far
easier to spot in a plot than in a column of numbers. Let's plot some key variables to understand
their distributions and relationships.

### Example 1: Histogram

Histograms are useful for visualizing the distribution of a single numeric variable. Let's look
at age.

```{webr-r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Age", x = "Age", y = "Frequency")
```

**How to read this:** the x-axis is age, split into 5-year bins (that's what `binwidth = 5` does);
the y-axis is a count — how many participants fall into each bin. Taller bars mean more people at
that age range. From this single plot, you can read off roughly where the minimum and maximum ages
are (the leftmost and rightmost bars with any height at all), and see at a glance where the bulk of
participants' ages fall — which, here, looks like it's concentrated in the younger-to-middle adult
range, with progressively fewer people as age increases. You should also be able to spot a bar (or
bars) sitting well off to the right, separated from the rest of the distribution — that's a visual
signal of an age **outlier**, the same implausible values we're about to deal with directly below.

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn"}
Before we get to age's outlier problem below, get a look at our primary *exposure* variable's
distribution. Build a histogram of **`hrlctree`** (tree canopy cover) — start by copying the age
histogram code above and just swapping in `hrlctree`.

**One thing you'll need to change: `binwidth`.** A `binwidth` of `5` made sense for `age`, which
spans roughly 18 to 116 years — but `hrlctree` is a *proportion*, ranging only from 0 to 1. A bin
5 units wide would swallow the entire variable into a single bar, telling you nothing. Try a much
smaller value, like `0.05`, instead.

More generally, whenever you build a histogram of a new variable: first check its rough range (a
quick `summary()` or `range()` will tell you), then pick a `binwidth` that divides that range into
something like 10–30 bins. Too few bins hides the shape of the distribution; too many makes it
look noisy. There's no single "correct" binwidth — this is a judgment call you refine by trying a
value, looking at the plot, and adjusting.
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here — histogram of hrlctree

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Solution — click to reveal"}
```{webr-r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = hrlctree)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "forestgreen", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Tree Canopy Cover", x = "Tree canopy cover (proportion)", y = "Frequency")
```
Most tracts should cluster at fairly low canopy values with a long right tail toward a handful of
much greener tracts — worth keeping in mind before you characterize this variable for your own
project.
:::

Okay, back to age. Some of the values we see for age look suspicious — the ages > 110 are very suspect. This is the
third error type from earlier: an **outlier**. Let's recode those with age > 105 to be missing.
(Another option would be to recode these to some high but plausible number, e.g. 100.)

There's a trade-off here: we gain more missing values, or we introduce more uncertainty. This is a
balancing act you'll have to consider as you move forward with your own data analysis. Like most
things, there isn't necessarily one "right" answer — just be thoughtful, and document your choice.

Our new recoded age variable will be called `r_age`:

```{webr-r}
data$r_age <- ifelse(data$age > 105, NA, data$age)
```

We can check the number of missing values in the recoded and original age variables:

```{webr-r}
table(is.na(data$age))
table(is.na(data$r_age))
```

That is, we now have **four additional** missing observations, because there were four individuals
with ages > 105 — we have set these to missing. (Original missing age count: 3. After recoding: 7.
3 + 4 = 7 — the recode didn't touch anyone who wasn't already missing or above the 105 cutoff.)

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn"}
Recall from Lesson 1 that `dplyr`'s `if_else()` (typically used inside `mutate()`) is another way
to do the same recoding `ifelse()` just did. Recreate `r_age` using `mutate()` and `if_else()`
instead, calling the new column `r_age2`, and confirm it matches `r_age` (hint: a table of
`r_age == r_age2`, or `identical()`, can confirm this — remember that `NA == NA` is `NA`, not
`TRUE`, so a simple `table()` of the comparison is often clearer than `identical()` here).
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here — recreate r_age using mutate() + if_else(), call it r_age2

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Solution — click to reveal"}
```{webr-r}
data <- data %>%
  mutate(r_age2 = if_else(age > 105, NA_real_, age))

table(data$r_age == data$r_age2, useNA = "ifany")
```

(Note: `if_else()` is stricter than base R's `ifelse()` about types — it needs `NA_real_` rather
than a plain `NA` here, since `age` is a decimal/"double" column. This is a common `if_else()`
gotcha worth remembering.)
:::

Let's recreate our histogram with the recoded age variable:

```{webr-r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = r_age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Recoded Age", x = "Recoded Age", y = "Frequency")
```

Our histogram no longer has the age outliers we observed earlier.

### Example 2: Boxplot

Boxplots are helpful for identifying outliers and comparing distributions across categories.

Let's look at the distribution of age by gender.

```{webr-r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = gender, y = age)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "orange") +
  labs(title = "Age Distribution by Gender", x = "Gender", y = "Age")
```

**Question to consider:** What is the relationship between gender identity and age?

Let's look at high blood pressure, our primary outcome/dependent variable, by tree canopy cover
(our primary exposure/independent variable):

```{webr-r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = as.character(high_blood_pressure), y = hrlctree)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "orange") +
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by high blood pressure status", x = "High blood pressure", y = "Tree canopy cover")
```

Note the `as.character()` wrapped around `high_blood_pressure` in the code above. Why do we need
it? (Hint: try running the code without that wrapper. Hint 2: recall from the [Data
Codebook](codebook.qmd) how `high_blood_pressure` is coded/stored.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Why as.character()? — click to reveal"}
`high_blood_pressure` is stored as an **integer** 0/1 flag, not a category. Without
`as.character()`, `ggplot` treats it as a continuous numeric axis and tries to draw a single
boxplot (or a strange, mostly-empty range of "groups" between 0 and 1) rather than two separate
boxes for "0" and "1". Wrapping it in `as.character()` (or `factor()`) tells `ggplot` to treat it
as a categorical variable, so it draws one box per group as intended. This is the same
integer-flags-that-are-really-categories issue you first ran into with `str(data)` back in
Lesson 1.
:::

**Question to consider:** Based on what you see here, what is the relationship between high blood
pressure and % tree canopy cover?

::: {.callout-note}
Remember this is a **crude** estimate of the relationship — and, per Week 1, an association
(however real it looks here) is not the same thing as causation. Even if this boxplot shows a
clear pattern, several other explanations besides "tree canopy directly affects blood pressure"
are still on the table, including confounding by some third variable related to both. We'll
return to formal tools for evaluating that (regression models, and later in the course,
confounding assessment with causal diagrams) — for now, just describe what you see.
:::

Let's also look at tree canopy cover by gender:

```{webr-r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = gender, y = hrlctree)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "orange") +
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by gender", x = "Gender", y = "Tree canopy cover")
```

**Question to consider:** Based on what you see here, what is the relationship between gender
identity and % tree canopy cover? Why might this matter within the context of our study question?

Let's also look at tree canopy cover by education:

```{webr-r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = education, y = hrlctree)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "orange") +
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by education", x = "Education", y = "Tree canopy cover")
```

**Question to consider:** Based on what you see here, what is the relationship between personal
educational attainment and % tree canopy cover? Why might this matter within the context of our
study question?

::: {.callout-note}
Keep these last two plots in mind. You just checked whether two different variables (gender,
education) are related to our exposure of interest. That's exactly the first step in thinking
about **confounding** — a topic the course returns to formally in Week 5. A variable can only
confound a relationship if it's associated with *both* the exposure and the outcome; here you've
just checked the "associated with the exposure" half for two candidates. Not every variable you
check will turn out to matter — and that's useful information too.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn"}
Let's check one more candidate variable, this time against a different outcome. Build a boxplot of
**`hrlctree`** by **`mental_health`** status (remember: you'll need `as.character()` or `factor()`
around `mental_health`, for the same reason as `high_blood_pressure` above).
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here — boxplot of hrlctree by mental_health status

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Solution — click to reveal"}

### Example 3: Scatter Plot

Scatter plots are useful for exploring relationships between two numeric variables. Let's look at
the relationship between percentage of the census tract living in poverty and tree canopy cover:

```{webr-r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = pov_allage, y = hrlctree)) +
  geom_point(color = "purple") +
  labs(title = "% living in poverty vs. tree canopy cover", x = "% living in poverty", y = "% tree canopy")
```

**Question to consider:** Based on what you see, what do you conclude about the overall
relationship between living in a tract with higher % poverty and % tree canopy? Stated another
way, what is the general shape and direction of this relationship?

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn"}
Scatter plots are also a good sanity check when a dataset has two variables that *should* be
related. This dataset has two different greenness measures: `hrlctree` (tree canopy cover, linked
in during data creation) and `X2015_NDVI` (the NDVI value you yourself merged in during Lesson 1).
Build a scatter plot of `hrlctree` (x-axis) against `X2015_NDVI` (y-axis). Do they move together
the way you'd expect two measures of the same underlying thing to?
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here — scatter plot of hrlctree vs. X2015_NDVI

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Solution — click to reveal"}
```{webr-r}
ggplot(data, aes(x = hrlctree, y = X2015_NDVI)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen") +
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover vs. NDVI", x = "Tree canopy cover", y = "NDVI")
```
A clear positive relationship here is a reassuring sign — two independently sourced measures of
"how green is this place" agreeing with each other is exactly the kind of cross-check worth doing
before you build an argument around either one.
:::

### Example 4: Summary Table of Key Metrics

We can also create summary tables that group data by a categorical variable. Suppose we want to
summarize average age by gender:

```{webr-r}
summary_table <- data %>%
  group_by(gender) %>%
  summarize(
    avg_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_age = max(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_age = min(age, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

print(summary_table)
```

**Question to consider:** Compare the results from this summary table to the boxplot you made
earlier (age stratified by gender). Do you find one more useful than the other? Why?

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Your Turn"}
Build a similar summary table, but (a) group by **`education`** instead of `gender`, (b) summarize
**`hrlctree`** instead of `age`, and (c) add the **median** alongside the mean, max, and min.
:::

```{webr-r}
# Your code here — summary table of hrlctree by education, including the median

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="💡 Solution — click to reveal"}
```{webr-r}
tree_by_education <- data %>%
  group_by(education) %>%
  summarize(
    avg_tree = mean(hrlctree, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_tree = median(hrlctree, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_tree = max(hrlctree, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_tree = min(hrlctree, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

print(tree_by_education)
```
:::

You now have a working toolkit for characterizing a dataset: checking for missing values and
logical inconsistencies, summarizing distributions, building frequency tables, and visualizing
relationships with histograms, boxplots, scatter plots, and grouped summary tables. That's exactly
what **Project Milestone 1** (due this week) asks you to start doing for your own chosen exposure
and outcome — pick your pair from this dataset, and run them through the same steps you just
practiced here.

Next week, we turn to **exposure assessment and misclassification** — how exposure gets measured
and coded, and what happens when that measurement isn't perfect. Before then, take a closer look
at the environmental exposure variables in the [Data Codebook](codebook.qmd) (tree canopy,
traffic density, crime, air/greenness measures) as you think about which one you want to build
your project around.

# ======================================================
# 🚀 Quick-Start Script for Your Own Project
# ======================================================

Everything above walked through each step one at a time, with the browser-only fetching code mixed
in. Below is a **single reusable script** — this is what you'd paste into a new `.R` or `.qmd`
file inside `EOH635_project/scripts/`, running on your own computer with `class_data_processed.csv`
already sitting in `data_processed/` (from Lesson 1). Swap in your own variable names wherever
you see `# <- CHANGE THIS`, and use it as a starting checklist for Milestone 1.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 💻 In your RStudio script

```r
# ---- Setup ----
library(tidyverse)

# ---- Read in your data ----
data <- read.csv(file.path("data_processed", "class_data_processed.csv"))

# ---- 1. Missing data: check every column at once ----
colSums(is.na(data))

# ---- 2. Logical inconsistencies: cross-tabulate variables that should agree ----
# Example template -- replace both variables with a pair relevant to your own project
age_group <- ifelse(data$age < 19, "Under 19", "19 or older")   # <- CHANGE THIS to your own condition
table(age_group, data$education)                                # <- CHANGE THIS to your own pair

# ---- 3. Outliers + summary statistics ----
summary(data)                                    # all variables
summary(data %>% select(where(is.double)))       # numeric variables only

# ---- 4. Frequency tables for categorical variables ----
table(data$education)                            # <- CHANGE THIS to your own categorical variables
prop.table(table(data$education)) * 100

# Every non-numeric variable at once:
non_numeric_data <- data %>% select(-where(is.double), -id, -year)
lapply(non_numeric_data, function(x) {
  if (is.factor(x) || is.character(x) || is.logical(x) || is.integer(x)) {
    counts <- table(x, useNA = "ifany")
    percentages <- prop.table(counts) * 100
    cbind(Count = counts, Percentage = percentages)
  } else {
    NULL
  }
})

# ---- 5. Recode an implausible value once you've found one ----
# Template, following the age > 105 example above:
data$r_age <- ifelse(data$age > 105, NA, data$age)   # <- CHANGE THIS to your own variable/cutoff

# ---- 6. Visualize a single continuous variable ----
ggplot(data, aes(x = age)) +                                    # <- CHANGE THIS to your exposure or outcome
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Age", x = "Age", y = "Frequency")

# ---- 7. Visualize your exposure-outcome relationship ----
# If your outcome is a 0/1 flag, wrap it in as.character() so ggplot treats it as a category:
ggplot(data, aes(x = as.character(high_blood_pressure), y = hrlctree)) +  # <- CHANGE THIS
  geom_boxplot(fill = "orange") +
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by high blood pressure status",
       x = "High blood pressure", y = "Tree canopy cover")

# If both your exposure and outcome are continuous, use a scatter plot instead:
ggplot(data, aes(x = pov_allage, y = hrlctree)) +                # <- CHANGE THIS
  geom_point(color = "purple") +
  labs(title = "% living in poverty vs. tree canopy cover",
       x = "% living in poverty", y = "% tree canopy")

# ---- 8. Check a candidate confounder against your exposure ----
ggplot(data, aes(x = education, y = hrlctree)) +                 # <- CHANGE THIS
  geom_boxplot(fill = "orange") +
  labs(title = "Tree canopy cover by education", x = "Education", y = "Tree canopy cover")

# ---- 9. Grouped summary table ----
data %>%
  group_by(education) %>%                                       # <- CHANGE THIS
  summarize(
    avg = mean(hrlctree, na.rm = TRUE),                          # <- CHANGE THIS
    median = median(hrlctree, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(hrlctree, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(hrlctree, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```
:::
